question: A 43-year-old woman visits her primary care provider complaining of fatigue. Although she has had it for several months, her fatigue has been worsening over the past few weeks. She has no other symptoms. Past medical history is significant for hypertension. She takes chlorthalidone, an oral contraceptive pill, and a multivitamin every day. Family history is noncontributory. She drinks about 1 bottle of wine every day and started taking a shot or two of whisky or vodka every morning before work to “clear out the cobwebs”. She was recently fired from her job. Today, her heart rate is 90/min, respiratory rate is 17/min, blood pressure is 110/65 mm Hg, and temperature is 36.7°C (98.1°F). On physical exam, she appears malnourished and anxious. Her conjunctiva are pale, and glossitis is noted on oral exam. Her heart has a regular rate and rhythm and her lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally. She has no gait or balance abnormalities. Lab results show a hemoglobin of 10 g/dL, with a mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 108 fl. Elevated level of which of the following will most likely to be found in this patient?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "macrocytic anemia" -> "MCV 108 fl" -> "vitamin B12 or folate deficiency" -> "elevated homocysteine" -> 85%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "macrocytic anemia" -> "MCV 108 fl" -> "vitamin B12 deficiency" -> "elevated methylmalonic acid" -> 75%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "macrocytic anemia" -> "MCV 108 fl" -> "alcohol use" -> "folate deficiency" -> "elevated homocysteine" -> 80%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "macrocytic anemia" -> "MCV 108 fl" -> "alcohol use" -> "possible vitamin B12 deficiency" -> "elevated methylmalonic acid" -> 70%
CHAIN: "Fatigue and glossitis" -> "macrocytic anemia" -> "MCV 108 fl" -> "malnutrition" -> "vitamin B12 or folate deficiency" -> "elevated homocysteine" -> 75%
enhanced_information: The patient presents with fatigue, glossitis, and macrocytic anemia (MCV 108 fl), which are indicative of either vitamin B12 or folate deficiency. Her alcohol use and malnourished state increase the likelihood of folate deficiency, which is commonly associated with elevated homocysteine levels. While both vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies can cause elevated homocysteine, only vitamin B12 deficiency leads to elevated methylmalonic acid. The evidence paths confirm that malnutrition can cause folic acid deficiency, supporting the likelihood of elevated homocysteine. Therefore, the most likely elevated substance in this patient is homocysteine, aligning with the consensus that alcohol use and malnutrition are more directly linked to folate deficiency rather than vitamin B12 deficiency in this context.
analysis: The patient presents with symptoms and lab findings suggestive of macrocytic anemia, specifically with an elevated mean corpuscular volume (MCV) of 108 fl. This type of anemia is commonly associated with deficiencies in vitamin B12 or folate. The patient's significant alcohol consumption and malnourished appearance increase the likelihood of folate deficiency, as alcohol interferes with folate metabolism and absorption. Both vitamin B12 and folate deficiencies can lead to elevated homocysteine levels, but only vitamin B12 deficiency results in elevated methylmalonic acid levels. Given the context of alcohol use and malnutrition, folate deficiency is more probable, which would result in elevated homocysteine levels. Therefore, the most likely elevated substance in this patient is homocysteine.
